```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
pal <- c(navy = "#2b3a67", teal = "#2a9d8f", orange = "#e76f51",
         gold = "#e9c46a", grey = "#bbbbbb")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))
set.seed(11)
```

## This afternoon {.center}

We are not running any software.

. . .

By the end you should be able to say, in your own words, where each number in a
count table came from.

## A sequencer returns text

```
@A00984:412:HTKJ7DSXX:1:1101:2645:1000 1:N:0:ACTGAGCG
TACGTAGGGTGCGAGCGTTGTCCGGATTTATTGGGCGTAAAGCGCGCGCAGGCGGTTTGTT
+
FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF,FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF,FFF
```

. . .

Millions of these per sample. A name, a sequence, and a quality score per base.

. . .

Everything that follows is an attempt to answer one question: **what was in the
tube, and how much of it?**

## Two experiments, two paths, one destination

```{r}
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 6
steps <- tribble(
  ~path, ~step, ~label,
  "16S", 1, "cervicovaginal\nswab",
  "16S", 2, "amplify the\n16S V3-V4 region",
  "16S", 3, "sequence",
  "16S", 4, "denoise into\nexact sequences",
  "16S", 5, "classify against\na reference",
  "16S", 6, "counts per\nspecies",
  "RNA", 1, "cervicovaginal\nswab",
  "RNA", 2, "capture mRNA,\nmake cDNA",
  "RNA", 3, "sequence",
  "RNA", 4, "align to the\nhuman genome",
  "RNA", 5, "count reads\nper gene model",
  "RNA", 6, "counts per\ngene"
) |>
  mutate(y = if_else(path == "16S", 2, 1),
         fill = case_when(step == 6 ~ pal[["navy"]],
                          path == "16S" ~ pal[["teal"]],
                          TRUE ~ pal[["orange"]]))

ggplot(steps, aes(step, y)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = step, xend = step + 0.98, y = y, yend = y),
               data = steps |> filter(step < 6),
               colour = pal[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.8,
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = fill), width = 0.86, height = 0.62, colour = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), colour = "white", size = 3.8, lineheight = 0.95,
            fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(2, 1), labels = c("16S", "RNA-seq"), limits = c(0.5, 2.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 16) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "grey25", hjust = 1,
                                   margin = margin(r = 10)))
```

Different biology, different software, same final object.

## 16S: one gene, every bacterium {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
The 16S ribosomal RNA gene is in every bacterium, and parts of it differ between
species.

::: {.incremental}
- amplify one variable region with PCR
- sequence only that amplicon
- group identical sequences together
- look each one up in a reference database
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 500)) |>
  mutate(conserved = 0.15 + 0.1 * sin(x * 3),
         variable = if_else(x > 3 & x < 5 | x > 7 & x < 8.5, 0.9, 0.15)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x)) +
  geom_area(aes(y = variable), fill = pal[["teal"]], alpha = 0.85) +
  annotate("text", x = 4, y = 1.05, label = "V3", size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 7.75, y = 1.05, label = "V4", size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 0.33, label = "conserved", size = 4, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "position along the 16S gene", y = "variation between species") +
  ylim(0, 1.15) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```
:::
:::

## What a 16S count means

A cell in the species table is: **the number of amplicon reads in this sample
that matched this species.**

. . .

That is not the number of bacteria. Between the cell and the count sit

::: {.incremental}
- how many copies of the 16S gene that species carries
- how well the primers bind to it
- how completely the cells lysed
- how deeply the sample was sequenced
:::

## RNA-seq: every gene, one organism {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.incremental}
- pull out messenger RNA
- copy it to cDNA and fragment it
- sequence the fragments
- find where each fragment belongs in the genome
- count fragments overlapping each gene
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
reads <- tibble(start = runif(26, 0, 9), y = rep(1:13, each = 2) * 0.07 + 0.25)
tibble(x = 0) |>
  ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 10, ymin = 0.05, ymax = 0.17,
           fill = pal[["grey"]]) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = c(1, 4.2, 7.5), xmax = c(2.6, 6, 9.2), ymin = 0.05, ymax = 0.17,
           fill = pal[["navy"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.8, y = 0.01, label = "exon", size = 4, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_segment(data = reads, aes(x = start, xend = start + 0.75, y = y, yend = y),
               colour = pal[["orange"]], linewidth = 1.6) +
  labs(x = "position along the gene", y = NULL) +
  xlim(0, 10) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```
:::
:::

## What an RNA-seq count means

A cell in the gene table is: **the number of fragments in this sample assigned
to this gene.**

. . .

Also not a molecule count. Between the transcript and the count sit

::: {.incremental}
- how long the gene is
- how well the capture chemistry worked
- whether the read could be placed uniquely
- how deeply the sample was sequenced
:::

## The sentence to remember {.center}

A count table is **not** a measurement of how much was there.

. . .

It is a measurement of how much was there, **relative to everything else in that
tube**, multiplied by how hard we looked.

## Which is why every analysis starts the same way

::: {.incremental}
1. How deeply was each sample sequenced?
2. Which features are we even able to see?
3. Only then: does anything differ between groups?
:::

. . .

Tomorrow morning is step 1 and step 2, on both tables at once.

## One more label we will keep {.smaller}

Our gene table was produced in **two sequencing batches**.

. . .

We could have hidden that. We left it in, because on Wednesday you will measure
how much of the table it explains, and the answer is uncomfortable.

. . .

Keep every technical label your sequencing facility gives you. You cannot check
for a problem you did not write down.
